diagnostic_evidence.quote: Here $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a differentiable interaction kernel that weighs the influence of neighbouring agents

issues.failure_explanation: The sentence asserts that solutions of the model converge to finitely many clusters in finite time. The paper's own model uses a differentiable (in fact C^2, compactly supported) kernel, so the right-hand side of (eq:MAsystem) is smooth in the state; a cluster configuration (groups of agents sharing one colour with no residual cross-interaction) is an equilibrium of this ODE, and by uniqueness for locally Lipschitz ODEs an equilibrium can only be approached as t→∞, never reached in finite time. The finite-time clustering results in the cited opinion-dynamics literature concern discontinuous (indicator/cut-off) interaction functions, not smooth kernels, so the claim is false for the model studied here.

failure_location.quote: Classical results for opinion dynamics models~\cite{MotschTadmor2014} ensure that, under mild assumptions on $\phi$, the solution converges to a finite number of clusters in finite time.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace 'in finite time' with convergence as t→∞ (approximate clusters for large finite T).
issues.overall_effect: Misstates the long-time behaviour of the core model (eq:MAsystem). Only the narrative motivation and the heuristic choice of the horizon T in Remark rmk:parameters lean on it; no theorem or algorithm formally uses finite-time convergence.
issues.title: Finite-time cluster formation is claimed for a smooth interaction kernel
issues.why_classification: A local wording weakening; every theorem, algorithm, and numerical claim is unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $\alpha > 0$. Then the functional $J : H^1(\Omega) \to \R$ in Definition \ref{def:cost_functional} has a unique global minimum.
\underset{\varepsilon \in \mathcal{E}}{\text{minimise}} \quad J(c(\,\cdot\, ,T; \varepsilon)) \quad \text{subject to \eqref{eq:MAsystem}-\eqref{eq:ellipsoid}}.
We define a cost functional based on the $L^2$ norm of the intensity gradient, establish the well-posedness of the problem, and derive the corresponding optimality system.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that Theorem thm:existence1 'ensures the well-posedness of the problem', and the introduction lists establishing 'the well-posedness of the problem' as a contribution. What Theorem thm:existence1 establishes is only existence and uniqueness of a minimiser of the static functional J over H^1(Ω). The problem the paper actually optimises is the Mayer problem (eq:OCP) over admissible controls ε∈ℰ, for which no existence (let alone uniqueness) result is given anywhere. The gap is mathematical, not expository: ε enters the dynamics nonlinearly through φ(r^ε), so the velocity set is nonconvex and standard Filippov/Cesari existence theory does not apply directly; existence of a classical optimal control may require relaxed controls.

failure_location.quote: The following result ensures the well-posedness of the problem

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either supply a genuine existence theorem for (eq:OCP) (nontrivial, likely requiring relaxation), or weaken the prose to say that Theorem thm:existence1 concerns only the static functional J and that well-posedness of (eq:OCP) is not addressed.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised well-posedness of the optimal control problem (eq:OCP) is unsupported; 'optimal controls' ε* are defined and computed throughout without any existence guarantee.
issues.title: Well-posedness is claimed for the optimal control problem but proved only for the static functional
issues.why_classification: The least repair withdraws an advertised claim while leaving the paper recognisably comparable; the alternative (an existence proof for (eq:OCP)) needs new nontrivial analysis. Not serious: no formal result or numerical experiment depends on it.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \tilde J(c,\lambda,\varepsilon) = \int_0^T \int_\Omega \lambda(x,t) \cdot [\partial_t c(x,t) - F(c(x,t), \varepsilon(t))]\ dx\ dt + J(c(\,\cdot\, ,T; \varepsilon)).
&=\int_\Omega \lambda(x,T)\, v(x,T)\ dx -  \int_\Omega \int_0^T [- \partial_t\lambda - \partial_c F(c,\varepsilon) \cdot \lambda]\, v\ dt dx +\\
\tilde J'(\varepsilon)[z] = \int_0^T \int_\Omega - \lambda(x,t) \cdot \partial_\varepsilon F(c(x,t), \varepsilon(t))\, dx \ z(t) \, dt = 0
\sum_i \lambda_i(t) \, \partial_{\varepsilon_x} F(c_i(t),\varepsilon(t))

issues.failure_explanation: With the augmented functional as written (multiplier λ on [∂_t c − F]), integration by parts gives δJ̃ = ∫_Ω[λ(T) − Δc(T) + α(c(T)−I)]v(T) + ∫∫[−∂_t λ − ∂_c F·λ]v, so stationarity forces λ(·,T) = Δc(·,T) − α(c(·,T)−I), the negative of the terminal condition stated in (eq:opt_system-b). The appendix's second display contains a compensating sign error (a spurious minus sign in front of the whole time integral), and the stated terminal condition does not follow even from that line. The same clash reappears for the control gradient: J̃'(ε)[z] is computed with the factor −∫λ·∂_εF, yet the displayed discrete functional gradient uses +Σ_i λ_i ∂_εF. The TV adjoint terminal condition (eq:new_adjoint) inherits the same flipped convention. Because the adjoint equation and (eq:opt_system-c) are homogeneous in λ, the zero set of the system equals the correct one and the two sign flips cancel in the implemented descent direction, but the derivation as written is mathematically incorrect.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Adopt one consistent multiplier convention, e.g. change (eq:augmented_cost) to ∫λ·[F − ∂_t c] + J (equivalently flip the sign of λ), and fix the integration-by-parts line in Appendix app; then (eq:opt_system-b), the discrete gradient, and (eq:new_adjoint) are all correct as printed.
issues.overall_effect: The formal derivation of the optimality system (eq:opt_system) (Appendix app) is wrong as written, and (eq:new_adjoint) propagates the same inconsistent sign convention. The solution set of the system and the algorithm's search direction are accidentally unaffected.
issues.title: Sign inconsistency between the augmented functional and the adjoint terminal condition, with a wrong sign step in the appendix derivation
issues.why_classification: A single sign change in one display plus the matching IBP line makes the whole derivation consistent; the optimality system's solutions, the algorithm, and every substantive claim survive unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \WHILE{ $J(\Pi_E(\varepsilon^{(j)} - \tau^{(k)}\, D^{(j)} )) \le J(\varepsilon^{(j)}) - c \,\tau^{(k)} |D^{(j)}|^2$ }
\STATE $\tau^{(k+1)} \gets \tau^{(k)}/b$

issues.failure_explanation: In the ELSE branch of Algorithm alg:dal, τ is enlarged while the sufficient-decrease inequality J(Π_E(ε−τD)) ≤ J(ε) − cτ|D|² holds; the loop exits at the first τ^{(k)} that violates it, and the algorithm then sets σ^{(j+1)} = τ^{(k)}, i.e. it accepts exactly a step size for which the Armijo condition fails (the last certified step would be τ^{(k−1)}). Hence, whenever the expansion branch is active, the returned step does not satisfy the sufficient-decrease condition that defines the advertised 'two-way Armijo backtracking line search'.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Accept the last successful trial, σ^{(j+1)} ← τ^{(k−1)} (equivalently, enlarge only after re-testing).
issues.overall_effect: The stated guarantee of the line search (an accepted step satisfying sufficient decrease of J) fails on the expansion branch; monotonicity of the cost along the written iteration is no longer ensured.
issues.title: Armijo expansion branch returns the first step size that fails the decrease condition
issues.why_classification: A one-line, forced index correction; the advertised algorithm and all numerical conclusions survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \IF{ $J(\Pi_E(\varepsilon^{(j)} - \sigma^{(j)}\, D^{(j)} )) > J(\varepsilon^{(j)}) - c \,\sigma^{(j)} |D^{(j)}|^2$ }
\STATE $D^{(j)} \gets \partial_\varepsilon F(c^{(j)},\varepsilon^{(j)}) \cdot \lambda^{(j)}$
which is essentially a steepest descent along the functional $J$

issues.failure_explanation: Every Armijo test in Algorithm alg:dal evaluates only trial points Π_E(ε^{(j)} − τ D^{(j)}), i.e. certifies decrease along −D^{(j)}, and the text describes the method as steepest descent; but the update line sets ε^{(j+1)} ← Π_E(ε^{(j)} + σ^{(j+1)} D^{(j)}), moving along +D^{(j)}. Whatever the sign convention for D, the step actually taken is the one the line search never tests. Under the paper's own adjoint/gradient conventions D^{(j)} equals the reduced gradient of the cost, so as written the update ascends rather than descends.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the update to ε^{(j+1)} ← Π_E(ε^{(j)} − σ^{(j+1)} D^{(j)}), the direction the line search certifies.
issues.overall_effect: As printed, Algorithm alg:dal does not implement the advertised projected steepest descent with Armijo line search; the accepted iterate has no decrease certificate, and the cost-stationarity stopping criterion (Remark rmk:convergence) may trigger spuriously.
issues.title: DAL control update moves in the direction opposite to the one the line search certifies
issues.why_classification: A single forced sign correction aligns the update with the tested direction; the stated method and all claims survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the compactly supported interaction kernel is given by the $C^2$ Wendland function \cite{Wendland1995}
each agent tends to align its state $c_i$ with the states of nearby agents whose intensities are similar

issues.failure_explanation: The kernel defined in (eq:kernel), φ(r) = (4r−1)(1−r)^4 on [0,1], equals −1 at r = 0 and is negative for r < 1/4. The C^2 Wendland function it is identified with (Wendland 1995; also the standard SPH choice in the cited Dehnen2012) is (1−r)^4_+(1+4r), strictly positive on [0,1). With the printed formula, pairs of agents at short spatial/tonal range enter (eq:MAsystem) with a negative weight, so nearby colours are driven apart (repulsion/anti-diffusion) instead of aligning. This contradicts the model's stated behaviour ('each agent tends to align its state with the states of nearby agents'), the diffusion-like smoothing interpretation of large ε_x, and the nonnegativity hypotheses of the consensus/clustering results invoked for the model.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restore the standard factor, φ(r) = (4r+1)(1−r)^4 on [0,1]; this single sign, pinned down by the paper's own citation, makes the kernel nonnegative and consistent with every use in the paper.
issues.overall_effect: As written, the interaction model (eq:MAsystem)-(eq:kernel) produces short-range repulsion in colour space, so the alignment/quantization narrative and the applicability of the cited clustering results fail; the derivative formulas (eq:dF_dc)–(eq:dF_depsc) remain internally consistent but describe the repulsive dynamics.
issues.title: The displayed 'C^2 Wendland' kernel is negative at short range, contradicting its stated role
issues.why_classification: One forced sign correction (the cited Wendland C^2 kernel) repairs the model; no inference, result, or numerical claim needs further change.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: L(u,v,\mu) = \int_\Omega |v(x)| + \mu(x) \cdot (v(x) - \nabla u(x)) + \frac{\rho}{2} |v(x) - \nabla u(x)|^2 + \frac{\alpha}{2}(u(x)- I(x))^2\ dx.
There exists a saddle point for the functional $L : H^1(\Omega) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \to \R$ defined in \eqref{eq:cost_tv_regular}.
The ensemble of these properties is sufficient to guarantee the existence of a saddle point in our setting (see for instance \cite[Chapter VI]{ET_1999}) and strong duality is directly implied by it.

issues.failure_explanation: (1) The asserted joint coercivity on H^1×L^2 is false: for μ=0 take smooth u_n with concentrating gradients (‖∇u_n‖_{L^1}=O(1), ‖∇u_n‖_{L^2}→∞, ‖u_n‖_{L^2}=O(1)) and v_n=∇u_n; then L(u_n,v_n,0)=‖∇u_n‖_{L^1}+(α/2)‖u_n−I‖² stays bounded while ‖(u_n,v_n)‖_{H^1×L^2}→∞, so sublevel sets are not weakly compact and the invoked direct-method step fails; nor do the listed separate convexity/coercivity properties suffice for the cited saddle-point theorem (Ekeland–Témam Ch. VI requires additional compactness/qualification hypotheses with an unconstrained dual variable). (2) Moreover the statement itself fails in the stated spaces for natural data: max_μ L(u,v,μ)=+∞ unless v=∇u, so a saddle point forces u* to minimise the ROF functional K over H^1(Ω); but inf_{H^1}K equals the BV minimum, which is unattained in H^1 whenever the unique ROF minimiser has jump discontinuities — e.g. I=1_B for a ball B of radius R with α>2/R gives u*=(1−2/(αR))1_B∉H^1. Jump (edge) solutions are precisely the regime the TV model is built for, so the existence claim fails in the motivating case.

failure_location.quote: Finally, as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:existence1}, it is immediate to show coercivity in the primal variables, ensuring that the minimum is attained in a weakly compact set.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reformulate the saddle problem in the standard ROF setting (u∈BV(Ω) with Du a measure, or an equivalent predual/finite-dimensional statement) and prove primal attainment in BV plus dual attainment via a qualification condition, as in the cited Chambolle–Lions; the alternative of keeping H^1 and assuming the minimiser is H^1-regular would exclude the advertised edge-preserving regime.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem thm:saddle_point, including the strong-duality equality (eq:duality), is unproved as written and false as stated for data whose ROF minimiser has edges; the 'no duality gap' justification invoked for Algorithm alg:admm inherits the gap. The finite-dimensional discretisation actually computed is unaffected, so the numerics stand.
issues.title: Saddle-point theorem: the coercivity claim is false, and primal attainment can fail in the stated H^1 spaces exactly in the edge regime
issues.why_classification: A contained but nontrivial repair (change of function-space setting plus a standard attainment argument) restores a recognisably comparable theorem; no other result depends on it and the discrete algorithm is unaffected. Not serious because the BV repair is standard, even cited, and preserves the advertised scope.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \underset{u \in H^1(\Omega),\, v \in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2)}{\min} \ \underset{\mu \in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) }{\max}  \quad L(u, v, \mu)
\mu(x) \cdot (v(x) - \nabla u(x))

issues.failure_explanation: The vanishing of ∫μ·(v*−∇u*) only says L(u*,v*,μ) is constant in μ; it does not make (u*,v*,μ) a saddle point for arbitrary μ. A saddle point also requires L(u*,v*,μ) ≤ L(u,v,μ) for all (u,v), which holds iff μ is a Lagrange multiplier for the constraint v=∇u — equivalently −μ(x)∈∂|·|(v*(x)) a.e., forcing ‖μ‖_{L^∞}≤1. Generic multipliers fail: for μ=0, min_v{|v|+(ρ/2)|v−g|²} < |g| whenever g≠0, hence min_{u,v}L(u,v,0) < K(u*) = L(u*,v*,0) whenever u* is nonconstant, so (u*,v*,0) is not a saddle point. The conclusion (non-uniqueness of the saddle multiplier) may hold, but the justification that all of L^2 becomes feasible is false.

failure_location.quote: In fact, when approaching the minimum point $(u^*,v^*)$ in the primal variables (which is unique), the term $\int_\Omega \mu \cdot (v^*-\nabla u^*)$ vanishes, so that any $\mu \in L^2(\Omega; \R^2)$ becomes feasible.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the explanation with the correct statement: the optimal multipliers form the (bounded, possibly non-singleton) set of μ satisfying the KKT/subgradient conditions.
issues.overall_effect: One explanatory paragraph about the saddle structure is mathematically false; no theorem, algorithm, or numerical claim depends on it.
issues.title: 'Any μ becomes feasible' is a false explanation of multiplier non-uniqueness
issues.why_classification: A local correction to a single remark; all formal content and guarantees survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \REQUIRE Initial guesses for the control $\varepsilon^{(0)}$ and the dual variable $\mu^{(0)}$, $\gamma > 0$
\STATE $j \gets 1$

issues.failure_explanation: Algorithm alg:admm initialises only μ^{(0)} and starts the loop at j=1; the update line computes μ^{(j+1)} from μ^{(j)}, so on the first pass it uses μ^{(1)}, which has never been assigned (in general μ^{(j)} is read before any assignment to it). As written the procedure is not well defined; the intended method-of-multipliers step is μ^{(j)} ← μ^{(j−1)} + γ(v^{(j)} − ∇c^{(j)}(·,T)) with the loop indices shifted accordingly.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reindex the dual update (right-hand side μ^{(j−1)}, assigned to μ^{(j)}) or start the loop at j=0.
issues.overall_effect: The pseudocode of Algorithm alg:admm is ill-defined from its first iteration; the intended ADMM iteration is nevertheless unambiguous.
issues.title: ADMM dual update references μ^{(j)} before it is ever defined
issues.why_classification: A forced one-index correction; the intended procedure and all reported results are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Finally, for the maximisation in the dual variable $\mu$, it is enough to perform a simple gradient ascent in the direction $v-\nabla u$, since the cost functional $L$ is linear in $\mu$.

issues.failure_explanation: The remark claims the two-way Armijo search of Algorithm alg:dal can choose the ascent step γ^{(j)} for the multiplier update. But, as the text itself states, L is linear in μ, so γ ↦ L(u,v,μ+γ(v−∇u)) is affine with slope ‖v−∇u‖²; a sufficient-increase Armijo test then holds for every γ>0 (and is vacuous when v=∇u), so the expansion loop of the two-way search would never terminate. Exact maximisation in μ is unbounded — the multiplier update of the method of multipliers is not a line-search maximisation — so the suggested variant is not a well-defined, let alone convergent, procedure.

failure_location.quote: The two-way line search utilised in Algorithm \ref{alg:dal} can also be employed to select a dynamic ascent step-size $\gamma^{(j)}$, on line 7 of Algorithm \ref{alg:admm}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Delete the remark (the fixed step, e.g. the standard choice γ comparable to ρ, is the correct method-of-multipliers update).
issues.overall_effect: A peripheral remark proposes an invalid algorithmic variant; the actual Algorithm alg:admm uses a fixed γ and is unaffected.
issues.title: An Armijo-type line search cannot select the dual ascent step, since L is affine in μ
issues.why_classification: Removing the peripheral remark loses nothing; the algorithm as actually run keeps a fixed step and all results stand.
